newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: S.Africa economy, rand seen higher - Manuel.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa economy, rand seen higher - Manuel.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said on Sunday that economic growth of 2.7 percent in 1997 was achievable despite last month's interest rate hike and he forecast a stronger rand next year.
"The macroeconomic framework that we tabled in June set a benchmark of about 2.7 percent in 1997...I remain of the opinion that it is within reach," he said in an interview.
Manuel's forecast contrasts with the view of economists polled by Reuters after the rate increase who predicted growth would slow to 2.2 percent in 1997 from 3.0 percent in 1996.
Manuel in June projected growth of 2.9 percent in 1997. It was not clear why there was a dicrepancy between this figure and 2.7 percent cited in the interview with Reuters.
South Africa's Reserve Bank late last month increased its key bank rate to 17 percent from 16 percent.
The move took many analysts by surprise and drew criticism from the South African Chamber of Business which described it as a severe blow to the economy.
But Manuel, who is in Australia for a trade conference, defended the central bank's decision as a necessary step toward economic stability.

"It is imperative that we do what is necessary to establish financial stability to match what remains a fairly bullish real economy and a capacity that we have in respect of fiscal policy to do what is necessary," he said.
He said the ministry was keen to build closer ties between the central bank and the government.
"We are looking for a cooperative style of management of the South African macroeconomy between the Reserve Bank and ourselves," he said.
Manuel asserted further confidence in the ability of South Africa's economy to mend by forecasting a stronger rand against major currencies in the near term.
"There is a fair amount of room for strengthening. I think generally it's been accepted that there's been an overshoot in the last period," he said.
"There's likely to be some strengthening over the next while," Manuel said when asked if he saw some strengthening in the rand over the next year or so.
Manuel said the currency was backed by a commitment by South Africa's central bank to support it over the long term.
"We have a constitutionally entrenched independent reserve bank that has a constitutional mandate to protect the long-term value of the currency," he said.
Manuel did not give a precise forecast for the rand.
Economists surveyed by Reuters last week forecast an exchange rate for the rand of 4.92 against the dollar by the end of 1997, and 5.17 by the end of the following year.
The rand, which has plummeted 30 percent against the dollar this year, was last traded at around 4.6130/4.6180.

Manuel declined to give a timeframe for the removal of foreign exchange controls, despite Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals' comments to Reuters last month that it was linked to the implementation of the government's macroeconomic strategy, a four to five-year process.
"I don't know why he said four to five years. The view I've held...is that it's a process shaped by circumstances rather than by some date pulled from a hat," Manuel said.
But he said the removal of exchange controls was tied to reserve levels which remain low.
"I think your reserve level is going to be key to that entire situation," Manuel said.
South Africa's official reserves rose slightly to 10.28 billion rand in October from 10.04 billion in September.
